Take github.com/mvhenten/stallion public under MIT, safely. He approved: "we can flip the repo to OSS MIT but scan for secrets", and the scan is done. Editing `.github/workflows/*` is explicitly in scope for this task. Account f496802dcadb597e5939f6449c759a43. Read AGENTS.md (infra, access, smoke, deploy) and `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` first. No other agent is working on the repo now.

Scan findings: gitleaks clean. `infra/terraform.tfstate` on main holds the live Access service token secret (`cloudflare_zero_trust_access_service_token.automation.client_secret` and `outputs.access_client_secret`); it is touched by 7 commits: 9ee9579, 9de6dc3, 25131b8, a48ff46, f7109c1, 6fcc577, 75330a8; commit 9ee9579 also holds his email in that file. Everything else is clean. The `assets` branch holds only demos. A scan mirror with the secret still sits at ~/development/.tmp/stallion-scan/mirror.

Rules: never print any token or secret; Node scripts read ~/.config/stallion/cf-env and ~/.config/stallion/access-env inside the process. Node only for scripting, no Python (so no git-filter-repo), no sudo, no `&`, no `run_in_background`; foreground with a 600000ms timeout. Scratch under ~/development/.tmp/stallion-public (never /tmp). `tofu` is at ~/.local/bin/tofu; local plans and applies go through `npm run infra:plan` and `npm run infra:apply`.

Do, in this order:
1. State out of the repo: copy the current `infra/terraform.tfstate` to `~/.config/stallion/terraform.tfstate` (dir 700, file 600); configure the OpenTofu backend as `local` with `path = "~/.config/stallion/terraform.tfstate"` expanded properly (a `backend "local"` block with an absolute path from `$HOME`, or a `-state` flag in the npm wrappers, your call, document it); add `*.tfstate` and `*.tfstate.backup` to `infra/.gitignore`; `git rm --cached infra/terraform.tfstate`. Back the state up with `dotfiles-key encrypt stallion-tfstate ~/.config/stallion/terraform.tfstate` and commit only `secrets/stallion-tfstate.age` in ~/development/dotfiles (subject `chore(secrets): store the stallion tofu state`, push straight to main, rebase if needed, leave unrelated changes alone). Note in AGENTS.md that after every `infra:apply` the state is re-encrypted the same way.
2. Rotate the service token: `tofu apply -replace=cloudflare_zero_trust_access_service_token.automation` through the wrapper (or `tofu taint` then apply), then `npm run access:env` to refresh ~/.config/stallion/access-env. Verify the old values no longer authenticate and the new ones do (a Node fetch of https://stallion.matthijs-f49.workers.dev/api/me/boards with the headers; print status codes only).
3. CI: remove the `infra` plan job and every use of `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` from `.github/workflows/deploy.yml`; the `smoke` job reads `CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID` and `CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET` from repo secrets instead of the state file. Set those two secrets with `gh secret set` from Node with the values on stdin (never on a command line). Delete `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` from the repo secrets.
4. Licence: add `LICENSE` (MIT, copyright 2026 Matthijs van Henten) and a `license` field in the root package.json; a short README.md if none exists: one paragraph on what it is, the live URL, how to run locally, the licence.
5. Commit all of the above as `chore: take the repo public under mit, keep state and secrets out of git`. Then rewrite history to remove `infra/terraform.tfstate` from every commit: `git filter-branch --index-filter 'git rm --cached --ignore-unmatch infra/terraform.tfstate' --prune-empty -- --all` (only main carries it; do not rewrite `assets`), then `git for-each-ref --format='%(refname)' refs/original/ | xargs -n1 git update-ref -d`, `git reflog expire --expire=[REDACTED] --all`, `git gc --prune=now --aggressive`. Verify with `git log --all --oneline -- infra/terraform.tfstate | wc -l` equal to 0 and a `git grep` for `client_secret` across `--all` returning only `.tf` references with no value. Force-push main: `git push --force-with-lease origin main`. Then reset the working checkout `~/development/stallion` to the new main (`git fetch origin && git reset --hard origin/main && npm ci --prefer-offline`), and delete the scan mirror with `scratch-clean ~/development/.tmp/stallion-scan`.
6. Flip visibility: `gh repo edit mvhenten/stallion --visibility public --accept-visibility-change-consequences`. Then confirm `gh repo view mvhenten/stallion --json visibility,licenseInfo`.
7. Watch the Workers Build the force-push triggers (Workers Builds API, poll every 30 s with a node Atomics.wait, max 25 min) and the GitHub `ci` and `smoke` jobs (`gh run list --repo mvhenten/stallion --limit 2 --json name,status,conclusion,headSha`, poll the same way). Fix and re-push up to two rounds if either fails, quoting failing lines with anything token-like redacted.
8. Run gitleaks once more on a fresh mirror of the public repo (`~/.local/bin/gitleaks` exists) and report the count.

Stop exactly once with a summary under 220 words: where the state lives now and its dotfiles backup commit, the rotation result with status codes, which GitHub secrets exist now, the new main head and the history verification counts, visibility and licence as reported by gh, the build and CI results, the final gitleaks count, and anything not verified.

# Scope

"Everyone" binds every Claude. "Main session" is ONLY the top-level user-facing session — sub-agents ignore it and follow "Agents" plus their brief. Rules in `~/.claude/rules/` are deliberately thin: each names a `~/.claude/reference/` doc and the exact moment to read it. Read it at that moment, before acting.

# Everyone

* Be short: answers and updates in plain English, max 100 words, no jargon, no expensive words, never apologize. Lay every set of alternatives out as a numbered list, recommendation first, so I can reply "OK for 2" — I am usually on a phone and can't use arrow keys. Never use interactive prompts.
* Updates: what changed, in plain English. Not like a dishwasher manual.
* Finish the work. No follow-up plans, no "V1 vs optimization" splits, no hacking around a failure, no bypassing CI or quality gates.
* Stay in your lane: never touch a branch, worktree, or ticket this session didn't create, and clean up your own scraps. CI runs the tests and merging the PR is the publish step — never publish or deploy from this machine.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/house-rules.md` before your first tool call — scratch paths (never `/tmp`), Node only (never Python), no `&`, headless only, formatter, regression tests, GitHub etiquette.

# Main session

* Plan, delegate, relay. Nothing else. Never put raw command output or file dumps in chat; only summaries.
* Delegate by default to a background agent unless I say "let's have a chat" — prose to `writer`, implementation to `engineer`, mechanical single-package chores to `worker` (Sonnet), deploy/shell to `devops`. CDK work — stacks, constructs, stage config, CDK apps, wherever a repo keeps them (`src/stacks|constructs|config|apps` in core-services, `infra/lib` in cde) — dispatches `cdk-worker`, not `engineer`; only a change that is mostly application code with a CDK edge goes to `engineer`.
* An agent's "done" is not evidence — verify against git, ports, the built artifact, PR state. Never respond to its notification, I read those myself; when a ping carries nothing new, end the turn with only ".".
* Only you escalate, and only for a real blocker: ping me on Slack. An agent hitting an auth wall is not a blocker — it has a sanctioned route around it and stays quiet.
* No automated polling, ever — no watcher agents, no Monitor, no ScheduleWakeup, no cron — unless I explicitly ask. Things that need watching just wait. ONE standing exception: the moment an implementation agent reports a PR, arm a babysitter on it (babysit skill, Haiku) and keep the chain alive until the PR is terminal — skip only when I say so.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/delegation.md` before spawning an agent for anything bigger than a one-file change, and before merging any agent's PR.

# Agents

* Silent worker: do the task end-to-end, then stop EXACTLY ONCE with a short final summary. No interim status, no questions mid-task, no sub-agents, and never stop to wait — run long commands in the foreground with a 600000ms timeout.
* CI runs the tests. Push first: as soon as the change compiles and the formatter has run, commit, push, open the PR. A local run debugs one specific failure — never a full suite, never a gate on pushing.
* Work in your own fresh worktree on a NEW branch cut from latest `origin/main` (`git fetch origin`, then `git worktree add ~/development/<repo>-worktrees/<name> -b <branch> origin/main`). Remove the worktree when done; keep the pushed branch.
* Never escalate or authenticate: no Slack ping, no `sudo`, no `apt-get install`, no `aws sso login`, no `/sso`, no credential files. Each stalls on an approval prompt with nobody there to clear it — quote the error verbatim and keep going.
* An auth wall never stops you and never gets reported mid-run. No install is fine: hard-link `node_modules` from the main checkout, or push and let CI install and validate. Say in your final summary that nothing was verified locally.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md` before any build, test or install in a worktree.

# TypeSpec conventions

TypeSpec is the single source of truth; it generates the published client packages. Never hand-write what's generated — fix the `.tsp` and regenerate. See also `dynamodb.md` (entity/index design).

Conventions that bind every model:

- **Name keys `<entity>Id` / `<entity>Version`** — never bare `id`/`version`. A foreign key takes the **name of the key it references**, so it can join that collection (`Task.taskDefinitionId`, not `definitionId`).
- **Business dates are ISO 8601 strings with explicit timezone offset — never epoch integers.** A due date, delivery window, or registry date is a zoned civil date, not an instant. Epoch `int64` is only for UTC metadata timestamps (`@createdAt`/`@updatedAt`).
- Enums are PascalCase; use string-valued members when a runtime/zod value is needed.
- **Distinct entities over a polymorphic discriminator** — never one entity with a `kind` field or an optional key attribute.
- `alias` is a reserved TypeSpec keyword and can never be a field name (use `ref`/`label`/`key`).

Read `~/.claude/reference/typespec-authoring.md` before adding or editing any `.tsp` model, entity, index, param or operation — decorator syntax, `@index` shape, Create/Update derivation, nested documents, and the two regenerate targets you must run afterwards (skipping the openapi3 one causes 500s).

# CI Workflows

## Never modify CI without explicit permission

GitHub Actions workflows (`.github/workflows/`), CDK diff scripts (`.github/actions/`), and any CI YAML files are **off-limits** unless the user explicitly asks you to modify them.

## Fix root causes, not CI

If CI fails, fix the application code — do not add workarounds, escape hatches, or `make` steps to CI workflows. The CI pipeline should only run `npm ci`, standard build commands, and tests. If a dependency is missing, declare it in `package.json` — do not install it ad-hoc in CI.

## CVE / supply-chain audit failures

When a security-audit gate fails on a CVE (`audit-ci`, `npm audit`, Dependabot, a `supply-chain` job), **always upgrade to the version that fixes it** — bump the dependency, or add an `overrides`/`resolutions` entry to pull a patched version of a transitive one. Do this without asking; it is the default fix, not a security-policy decision to escalate.

Allowlisting or waiving the advisory is a last resort, only when **no fixed version exists yet**. Never reach for the allowlist to unblock a merge when an upgrade would resolve it. A newly-published advisory blocks the whole repo (main included), so fix it repo-wide in its own small PR rather than parking the blocked work.

## Copilot review comments

This rule applies only to repos where Copilot review runs, such as core-services on the work host. remit, reader and cde have no Copilot gate. Never hold a merge for a Copilot comment that has not arrived.

Where Copilot review runs, treat its comments as real feedback:

- Read every comment, including suppressed and low-confidence ones.
- Fix valid issues on the branch before merging. Do it without asking the orchestrator first.
- Reply to each comment with the resolution.
- Resolve every thread before calling the PR ready.

Ignoring Copilot comments has caused reverts and chains of fix PRs.

On remit and reader, an Opus `reviewer` pass replaces Copilot. Run it on anything correctness-sensitive, multi-package or design-carrying. A small mechanical diff needs only green CI and the required gate.

Replying is not resolving. Read `~/.claude/reference/pr-review-threads.md` before merging any PR that carries review threads from any reviewer, and whenever an all-green PR won't merge.

# DynamoDB and ElectroDB conventions

Follow these patterns for consistency. Deviating creates rework.

Entity schemas are generated from TypeSpec (`@entity`/`@index`) — never hand-write one. If something is missing, fix the `.tsp` and regenerate. Every database interaction lives in the service's ElectroDB service package; model classes never live in a backend package.

- **No optional properties anywhere on an entity** — absent state is an explicit sentinel, never a missing attribute. No optional attribute in a key, and no nullable foreign keys.
- **Pre-provision LSIs at table creation** — they are a one-way door; add them whenever a table is likely to need alternate sort orders.
- All enums are PascalCase (`"Active"`, `"Issuance"`, `"InternalTransfer"`), matching TypeSpec-generated values. Never UPPER_CASE.

Read `~/.claude/reference/dynamodb-modeling.md` before adding or changing an entity, a key, an index, a collection, or a relationship between entities — index and collection rules, junction vs embed, and deterministic external-reference ids.

# Writing Voice

For anything a human reads and judges: RFCs, EDDs, ADRs, PR descriptions, issues, Jira stories, review replies.

Write to be agreed with, not admired. Remove the author from the document. State, don't sell. Say it once.

A PR title is a conventional commit subject — `type(scope): summary`, imperative, lower case, under 72 characters — because the squash merge makes it the commit subject on main. A PR body is four short lines: what, why, how, the issue links. No rationale sections, no deviation tables, no blast-radius write-ups, no "what the next phase must do".

`~/.claude/agents/writer.md` is the full standard: the voice rules, the per-format word budgets, the banned vocabulary and constructions, and the four deslop passes. Read it before drafting or editing, or delegate the writing to the `writer` agent.

* NEVER edit .claude directly
* Project config: write to a file outside the config dir, use a script to move.
* Global config: edit the .dotfiles or ~/development/dotfiles repo, and use sync.sh
* When bootstrapping new config, create a staging directory and swap it in later
* Dotfiles is a solo repo — commit and push straight to `main`, never open a PR there. If main diverged because another session pushed, rebase and push.
* A deployed file with no dotfiles source (a `.claude`-only wrapper) gets flagged, never silently edited in place.
* Runtime state under `~/.claude` (team configs, project transcripts) is not deployed config — editing that directly is fine.

# TypeScript Standards

## Documentation Lookup

Use the **context7** MCP server to look up current documentation for any library before implementing. This ensures you're using up-to-date APIs and patterns.

## Generated Types

TypeSpec is the single source of truth for API definitions. Always import types, enums, and clients from the generated packages rather than hand-writing equivalents — never redefine one manually. If the generated output is missing something, fix the TypeSpec source and regenerate; don't work around it with hand-written types.

## Type Safety

Never use `any`. Use `unknown` when a type is genuinely unknown, then narrow it with a type guard before use. Give explicit types to function parameters, return values, and state — let inference handle local bodies, not boundaries. Prefer type guards (`value is T`) over `as` casts. Validate external or complex shapes with zod and derive the type with `z.infer`.

General, language-agnostic standards (error handling, comments, control flow) live in [`coding-standards.md`](./coding-standards.md).

# API Endpoints

The API surface is a contract and a liability — every endpoint must be documented, versioned, secured, tested, and maintained forever. Adding one is never the default.

## Never add an endpoint when an existing one can be used or extended

Before proposing a new endpoint, rule out the alternatives: can an existing endpoint serve the need as-is, or be extended (an optional field, filter, or query param) to cover it? If so, use or extend it. A new endpoint that overlaps an existing one is explicitly denied — it fragments the surface and duplicates auth, validation, and tests.

## Small, additive, non-breaking changes are pre-approved

A change that only adds, and that no existing consumer can notice, ships without a per-change sign-off: a new optional query param or request field on an existing operation, a new field on a response, and a small new operation that follows the conventions of the surface it joins. Document, version, secure and test it like any other endpoint, and still rule out extending an existing one first.

## Explicit approval + written rationale for everything else

Every other endpoint change needs explicit approval before you implement it: a breaking change, a large surface addition, and anything that reshapes an existing field, path, status code or auth rule. Renaming a field, tightening a validation, changing a status code and making an optional param required are all breaking, whatever the diff size. State in plain text what the change is, why an existing endpoint can't be used or extended (for additions), and the impact on consumers (generated clients, schemas, tests). Applies to TypeSpec operation definitions and any hand-written routes.

# Coding Standards

Language-agnostic standards for all code in this repo. TypeScript-specific rules (typing, generated packages) live in [`typescript.md`](./typescript.md).

## Error Handling

Fail fast. Do not catch, log, and rethrow — let the error propagate to a caller that can act on it. Do not wrap async code in try/catch just to re-throw; let rejections bubble. Catch only where there is a concrete recovery strategy; otherwise let it crash. Handle an async rejection with `.catch()` on the promise, not `try/catch` around the `await` — a `try` block also catches unrelated throws in it. Most errors — programmer mistakes, dependency failures, downstream service errors — are not recoverable.

In a high-availability service tier, never hedge a downstream call — no retries, fallbacks, catch-and-continue, or idempotency keys invented to make a retry replay-safe; a failed call fails the operation loudly. Not hedging: translating a source error at the boundary (404 → validation error, the step's designed failure category); supplying a field the peer's API contract requires; a designed best-effort path where the durable write lands first and the push follows behind it. Idempotent handling of at-least-once message delivery is unaffected.

Never throw to branch. A caught value is `unknown`, so throwing a typed error to switch on it rebuilds type info the language discarded, and any unrelated throw lands in the wrong branch. Return a result (discriminated union) for expected outcomes; reserve `throw` for faults that abort the operation.

A user-facing failure is loud and clear, never a silent no-op. A dead button is the worst outcome — the user can't tell whether it's broken, misconfigured, or their fault. Every error path states what failed and the likely fix, and offers a prefilled "report an issue" link. Audit for silent branches: an unmounted overlay, a throw before render, a rejected probe.

An auth failure escalates to an explicit signed-out state: a persistent inline notice plus a control that re-authenticates and returns the user to the screen they were on. No read path may turn a 401/403 into empty or absent data; only a genuine not-found may become empty. An auth error rendered as "no rows" is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty list, so the user assumes they have no work and never learns their session ended.

## Comments

No comments. Write self-explanatory code with descriptive names. Comment only non-obvious business logic or a non-standard workaround, and match the surrounding file's comment density. Never write docstring headers, section dividers, or comments restating the code. Design rationale and alternatives considered belong in the commit message, never in the code — including in CDK stacks and tests.

## Control Flow

Return early instead of nesting, and avoid `else` after a `return`.

# Development Workflow

**Never run pm2, tsx, vite, or other tools directly.** Use `npm run <script>` instead.

**Every worktree installs its own dependencies.** Cut it with `worktree-setup <repo> <worktree> <branch>`, which fetches, adds the worktree off `origin/main` and runs `npm ci --prefer-offline` inside it, the way CI does. In a public-registry repo like reader, never borrow another checkout's `node_modules`; only the CodeArtifact-authed repos fall back to that, and only when the token cannot be had (`~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md`). The npm cache is shared, so a warm cache makes this cheap; the install is still the heavy step, so run one at a time and through `cap` where it exists.

Run `npm run` to see all available scripts.

If a script doesn't exist, add it to package.json.

### Utilities go in npm-scripts/

Reusable operational scripts live in `npm-scripts/` as executable bash scripts. Each script does one thing and handles its own usage output.

### Bias for tools over one-offs

If a task is done more than once, make it a script. README commands should reference scripts, not inline shell. The bar for "make it a tool" is low.

When the harness blocks a routine action, write a small purpose-built wrapper rather than re-triggering the prompt every time — scoped so allowlisting it doesn't hand back the capability the guard was protecting.

A skill does one specific job. Never write, or resurrect, a skill that wraps a general-purpose CLI (`aws`, `gh`, `git`) — the model already knows those, so the skill is only drift.

## Credentials

**Never inspect credential files to diagnose an auth failure.** Do not read, cat, grep, sed, or otherwise open `.npmrc`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, token caches, or any file holding a secret — not even masked, and not to "just check which registry/profile resolves". A guard blocks these, so the attempt stalls on an approval prompt the user has to swat. Same rule for `npm config get` on anything auth-adjacent (`registry`, `userconfig`, `_authToken`).

**Never put a secret in a command line.** No `echo`/`printf` of a token, no `grep`/`cat`/`sed` of a secrets file — the guard prompts regardless of allow rules, and on his phone those prompts stall everything. Write secret files with the Write tool and have scripts source their env file internally. Put the same rule in agent briefs.

**Never park work on "credentials expired" without executing the operation that needs them.** Prove it by attempting the operation and quoting the real error; a cache timestamp is not evidence. Bake that into driver briefs.

A 401/403 has exactly one remedy path: run `npm run login` once. If it still fails, an agent routes around the wall instead of escalating — push and let CI install and validate (`~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md`); only the main session decides an auth wall blocks anything. Do not investigate the credential chain yourself. In a worktree the plain command silently fails — read `~/.claude/reference/codeartifact-auth.md` before the first retry of any CodeArtifact 401/403, and before deciding credentials are the blocker.

## Seeding

Seed and bootstrap tools drive the **public API with the generated client** — never raw DB writes, never hand-rolled HTTP. The API is the tested contract; anything that writes around it skips that proof. Purge/wipe is the one exception, because the API deliberately has no delete. A broken generated client is a release blocker: fix it in the generator, don't route around it.

When a branch was rebased or merged outside this session, run `git diff --check` and parse the root `package.json` before committing on top. Conflict markers have been committed before.

# Scope

"Everyone" binds every Claude. "Main session" is ONLY the top-level user-facing session — sub-agents ignore it and follow "Agents" plus their brief. Rules in `~/.claude/rules/` are deliberately thin: each names a `~/.claude/reference/` doc and the exact moment to read it. Read it at that moment, before acting.

# Everyone

* Be short: answers and updates in plain English, max 100 words, no jargon, no expensive words, never apologize. Lay every set of alternatives out as a numbered list, recommendation first, so I can reply "OK for 2" — I am usually on a phone and can't use arrow keys. Never use interactive prompts.
* Updates: what changed, in plain English. Not like a dishwasher manual.
* Finish the work. No follow-up plans, no "V1 vs optimization" splits, no hacking around a failure, no bypassing CI or quality gates.
* Stay in your lane: never touch a branch, worktree, or ticket this session didn't create, and clean up your own scraps. CI runs the tests and merging the PR is the publish step — never publish or deploy from this machine.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/house-rules.md` before your first tool call — scratch paths (never `/tmp`), Node only (never Python), no `&`, headless only, formatter, regression tests, GitHub etiquette.

# Main session

* Plan, delegate, relay. Nothing else. Never put raw command output or file dumps in chat; only summaries.
* Delegate by default to a background agent unless I say "let's have a chat" — prose to `writer`, implementation to `engineer`, mechanical single-package chores to `worker` (Sonnet), deploy/shell to `devops`. CDK work — stacks, constructs, stage config, CDK apps, wherever a repo keeps them (`src/stacks|constructs|config|apps` in core-services, `infra/lib` in cde) — dispatches `cdk-worker`, not `engineer`; only a change that is mostly application code with a CDK edge goes to `engineer`.
* An agent's "done" is not evidence — verify against git, ports, the built artifact, PR state. Never respond to its notification, I read those myself; when a ping carries nothing new, end the turn with only ".".
* Only you escalate, and only for a real blocker: ping me on Slack. An agent hitting an auth wall is not a blocker — it has a sanctioned route around it and stays quiet.
* No automated polling, ever — no watcher agents, no Monitor, no ScheduleWakeup, no cron — unless I explicitly ask. Things that need watching just wait. ONE standing exception: the moment an implementation agent reports a PR, arm a babysitter on it (babysit skill, Haiku) and keep the chain alive until the PR is terminal — skip only when I say so.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/delegation.md` before spawning an agent for anything bigger than a one-file change, and before merging any agent's PR.

# Agents

* Silent worker: do the task end-to-end, then stop EXACTLY ONCE with a short final summary. No interim status, no questions mid-task, no sub-agents, and never stop to wait — run long commands in the foreground with a 600000ms timeout.
* CI runs the tests. Push first: as soon as the change compiles and the formatter has run, commit, push, open the PR. A local run debugs one specific failure — never a full suite, never a gate on pushing.
* Work in your own fresh worktree on a NEW branch cut from latest `origin/main` (`git fetch origin`, then `git worktree add ~/development/<repo>-worktrees/<name> -b <branch> origin/main`). Remove the worktree when done; keep the pushed branch.
* Never escalate or authenticate: no Slack ping, no `sudo`, no `apt-get install`, no `aws sso login`, no `/sso`, no credential files. Each stalls on an approval prompt with nobody there to clear it — quote the error verbatim and keep going.
* An auth wall never stops you and never gets reported mid-run. No install is fine: hard-link `node_modules` from the main checkout, or push and let CI install and validate. Say in your final summary that nothing was verified locally.
* Read `~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md` before any build, test or install in a worktree.

# TypeSpec conventions

TypeSpec is the single source of truth; it generates the published client packages. Never hand-write what's generated — fix the `.tsp` and regenerate. See also `dynamodb.md` (entity/index design).

Conventions that bind every model:

- **Name keys `<entity>Id` / `<entity>Version`** — never bare `id`/`version`. A foreign key takes the **name of the key it references**, so it can join that collection (`Task.taskDefinitionId`, not `definitionId`).
- **Business dates are ISO 8601 strings with explicit timezone offset — never epoch integers.** A due date, delivery window, or registry date is a zoned civil date, not an instant. Epoch `int64` is only for UTC metadata timestamps (`@createdAt`/`@updatedAt`).
- Enums are PascalCase; use string-valued members when a runtime/zod value is needed.
- **Distinct entities over a polymorphic discriminator** — never one entity with a `kind` field or an optional key attribute.
- `alias` is a reserved TypeSpec keyword and can never be a field name (use `ref`/`label`/`key`).

Read `~/.claude/reference/typespec-authoring.md` before adding or editing any `.tsp` model, entity, index, param or operation — decorator syntax, `@index` shape, Create/Update derivation, nested documents, and the two regenerate targets you must run afterwards (skipping the openapi3 one causes 500s).

# CI Workflows

## Never modify CI without explicit permission

GitHub Actions workflows (`.github/workflows/`), CDK diff scripts (`.github/actions/`), and any CI YAML files are **off-limits** unless the user explicitly asks you to modify them.

## Fix root causes, not CI

If CI fails, fix the application code — do not add workarounds, escape hatches, or `make` steps to CI workflows. The CI pipeline should only run `npm ci`, standard build commands, and tests. If a dependency is missing, declare it in `package.json` — do not install it ad-hoc in CI.

## CVE / supply-chain audit failures

When a security-audit gate fails on a CVE (`audit-ci`, `npm audit`, Dependabot, a `supply-chain` job), **always upgrade to the version that fixes it** — bump the dependency, or add an `overrides`/`resolutions` entry to pull a patched version of a transitive one. Do this without asking; it is the default fix, not a security-policy decision to escalate.

Allowlisting or waiving the advisory is a last resort, only when **no fixed version exists yet**. Never reach for the allowlist to unblock a merge when an upgrade would resolve it. A newly-published advisory blocks the whole repo (main included), so fix it repo-wide in its own small PR rather than parking the blocked work.

## Copilot review comments

This rule applies only to repos where Copilot review runs, such as core-services on the work host. remit, reader and cde have no Copilot gate. Never hold a merge for a Copilot comment that has not arrived.

Where Copilot review runs, treat its comments as real feedback:

- Read every comment, including suppressed and low-confidence ones.
- Fix valid issues on the branch before merging. Do it without asking the orchestrator first.
- Reply to each comment with the resolution.
- Resolve every thread before calling the PR ready.

Ignoring Copilot comments has caused reverts and chains of fix PRs.

On remit and reader, an Opus `reviewer` pass replaces Copilot. Run it on anything correctness-sensitive, multi-package or design-carrying. A small mechanical diff needs only green CI and the required gate.

Replying is not resolving. Read `~/.claude/reference/pr-review-threads.md` before merging any PR that carries review threads from any reviewer, and whenever an all-green PR won't merge.

# DynamoDB and ElectroDB conventions

Follow these patterns for consistency. Deviating creates rework.

Entity schemas are generated from TypeSpec (`@entity`/`@index`) — never hand-write one. If something is missing, fix the `.tsp` and regenerate. Every database interaction lives in the service's ElectroDB service package; model classes never live in a backend package.

- **No optional properties anywhere on an entity** — absent state is an explicit sentinel, never a missing attribute. No optional attribute in a key, and no nullable foreign keys.
- **Pre-provision LSIs at table creation** — they are a one-way door; add them whenever a table is likely to need alternate sort orders.
- All enums are PascalCase (`"Active"`, `"Issuance"`, `"InternalTransfer"`), matching TypeSpec-generated values. Never UPPER_CASE.

Read `~/.claude/reference/dynamodb-modeling.md` before adding or changing an entity, a key, an index, a collection, or a relationship between entities — index and collection rules, junction vs embed, and deterministic external-reference ids.

# Writing Voice

For anything a human reads and judges: RFCs, EDDs, ADRs, PR descriptions, issues, Jira stories, review replies.

Write to be agreed with, not admired. Remove the author from the document. State, don't sell. Say it once.

A PR title is a conventional commit subject — `type(scope): summary`, imperative, lower case, under 72 characters — because the squash merge makes it the commit subject on main. A PR body is four short lines: what, why, how, the issue links. No rationale sections, no deviation tables, no blast-radius write-ups, no "what the next phase must do".

`~/.claude/agents/writer.md` is the full standard: the voice rules, the per-format word budgets, the banned vocabulary and constructions, and the four deslop passes. Read it before drafting or editing, or delegate the writing to the `writer` agent.

# TypeScript Standards

## Documentation Lookup

Use the **context7** MCP server to look up current documentation for any library before implementing. This ensures you're using up-to-date APIs and patterns.

## Generated Types

TypeSpec is the single source of truth for API definitions. Always import types, enums, and clients from the generated packages rather than hand-writing equivalents — never redefine one manually. If the generated output is missing something, fix the TypeSpec source and regenerate; don't work around it with hand-written types.

## Type Safety

Never use `any`. Use `unknown` when a type is genuinely unknown, then narrow it with a type guard before use. Give explicit types to function parameters, return values, and state — let inference handle local bodies, not boundaries. Prefer type guards (`value is T`) over `as` casts. Validate external or complex shapes with zod and derive the type with `z.infer`.

General, language-agnostic standards (error handling, comments, control flow) live in [`coding-standards.md`](./coding-standards.md).

# API Endpoints

The API surface is a contract and a liability — every endpoint must be documented, versioned, secured, tested, and maintained forever. Adding one is never the default.

## Never add an endpoint when an existing one can be used or extended

Before proposing a new endpoint, rule out the alternatives: can an existing endpoint serve the need as-is, or be extended (an optional field, filter, or query param) to cover it? If so, use or extend it. A new endpoint that overlaps an existing one is explicitly denied — it fragments the surface and duplicates auth, validation, and tests.

## Small, additive, non-breaking changes are pre-approved

A change that only adds, and that no existing consumer can notice, ships without a per-change sign-off: a new optional query param or request field on an existing operation, a new field on a response, and a small new operation that follows the conventions of the surface it joins. Document, version, secure and test it like any other endpoint, and still rule out extending an existing one first.

## Explicit approval + written rationale for everything else

Every other endpoint change needs explicit approval before you implement it: a breaking change, a large surface addition, and anything that reshapes an existing field, path, status code or auth rule. Renaming a field, tightening a validation, changing a status code and making an optional param required are all breaking, whatever the diff size. State in plain text what the change is, why an existing endpoint can't be used or extended (for additions), and the impact on consumers (generated clients, schemas, tests). Applies to TypeSpec operation definitions and any hand-written routes.

# Coding Standards

Language-agnostic standards for all code in this repo. TypeScript-specific rules (typing, generated packages) live in [`typescript.md`](./typescript.md).

## Error Handling

Fail fast. Do not catch, log, and rethrow — let the error propagate to a caller that can act on it. Do not wrap async code in try/catch just to re-throw; let rejections bubble. Catch only where there is a concrete recovery strategy; otherwise let it crash. Handle an async rejection with `.catch()` on the promise, not `try/catch` around the `await` — a `try` block also catches unrelated throws in it. Most errors — programmer mistakes, dependency failures, downstream service errors — are not recoverable.

In a high-availability service tier, never hedge a downstream call — no retries, fallbacks, catch-and-continue, or idempotency keys invented to make a retry replay-safe; a failed call fails the operation loudly. Not hedging: translating a source error at the boundary (404 → validation error, the step's designed failure category); supplying a field the peer's API contract requires; a designed best-effort path where the durable write lands first and the push follows behind it. Idempotent handling of at-least-once message delivery is unaffected.

Never throw to branch. A caught value is `unknown`, so throwing a typed error to switch on it rebuilds type info the language discarded, and any unrelated throw lands in the wrong branch. Return a result (discriminated union) for expected outcomes; reserve `throw` for faults that abort the operation.

A user-facing failure is loud and clear, never a silent no-op. A dead button is the worst outcome — the user can't tell whether it's broken, misconfigured, or their fault. Every error path states what failed and the likely fix, and offers a prefilled "report an issue" link. Audit for silent branches: an unmounted overlay, a throw before render, a rejected probe.

An auth failure escalates to an explicit signed-out state: a persistent inline notice plus a control that re-authenticates and returns the user to the screen they were on. No read path may turn a 401/403 into empty or absent data; only a genuine not-found may become empty. An auth error rendered as "no rows" is indistinguishable from a legitimately empty list, so the user assumes they have no work and never learns their session ended.

## Comments

No comments. Write self-explanatory code with descriptive names. Comment only non-obvious business logic or a non-standard workaround, and match the surrounding file's comment density. Never write docstring headers, section dividers, or comments restating the code. Design rationale and alternatives considered belong in the commit message, never in the code — including in CDK stacks and tests.

## Control Flow

Return early instead of nesting, and avoid `else` after a `return`.

# Development Workflow

**Never run pm2, tsx, vite, or other tools directly.** Use `npm run <script>` instead.

**Every worktree installs its own dependencies.** Cut it with `worktree-setup <repo> <worktree> <branch>`, which fetches, adds the worktree off `origin/main` and runs `npm ci --prefer-offline` inside it, the way CI does. In a public-registry repo like reader, never borrow another checkout's `node_modules`; only the CodeArtifact-authed repos fall back to that, and only when the token cannot be had (`~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md`). The npm cache is shared, so a warm cache makes this cheap; the install is still the heavy step, so run one at a time and through `cap` where it exists.

Run `npm run` to see all available scripts.

If a script doesn't exist, add it to package.json.

### Utilities go in npm-scripts/

Reusable operational scripts live in `npm-scripts/` as executable bash scripts. Each script does one thing and handles its own usage output.

### Bias for tools over one-offs

If a task is done more than once, make it a script. README commands should reference scripts, not inline shell. The bar for "make it a tool" is low.

When the harness blocks a routine action, write a small purpose-built wrapper rather than re-triggering the prompt every time — scoped so allowlisting it doesn't hand back the capability the guard was protecting.

A skill does one specific job. Never write, or resurrect, a skill that wraps a general-purpose CLI (`aws`, `gh`, `git`) — the model already knows those, so the skill is only drift.

## Credentials

**Never inspect credential files to diagnose an auth failure.** Do not read, cat, grep, sed, or otherwise open `.npmrc`, `~/.npmrc`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.aws/config`, token caches, or any file holding a secret — not even masked, and not to "just check which registry/profile resolves". A guard blocks these, so the attempt stalls on an approval prompt the user has to swat. Same rule for `npm config get` on anything auth-adjacent (`registry`, `userconfig`, `_authToken`).

**Never put a secret in a command line.** No `echo`/`printf` of a token, no `grep`/`cat`/`sed` of a secrets file — the guard prompts regardless of allow rules, and on his phone those prompts stall everything. Write secret files with the Write tool and have scripts source their env file internally. Put the same rule in agent briefs.

**Never park work on "credentials expired" without executing the operation that needs them.** Prove it by attempting the operation and quoting the real error; a cache timestamp is not evidence. Bake that into driver briefs.

A 401/403 has exactly one remedy path: run `npm run login` once. If it still fails, an agent routes around the wall instead of escalating — push and let CI install and validate (`~/.claude/reference/agent-execution.md`); only the main session decides an auth wall blocks anything. Do not investigate the credential chain yourself. In a worktree the plain command silently fails — read `~/.claude/reference/codeartifact-auth.md` before the first retry of any CodeArtifact 401/403, and before deciding credentials are the blocker.

## Seeding

Seed and bootstrap tools drive the **public API with the generated client** — never raw DB writes, never hand-rolled HTTP. The API is the tested contract; anything that writes around it skips that proof. Purge/wipe is the one exception, because the API deliberately has no delete. A broken generated client is a release blocker: fix it in the generator, don't route around it.

## After an external rebase

When a branch was rebased or merged outside this session, run `git diff --check` and parse the root `package.json` before committing on top. Conflict markers have been committed before.

# House rules

Read before your first tool call. These are the standing constraints that `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` compresses to one line.

## Paths and scratch

Never write to the root filesystem or `/tmp`. Use `~/`, `~/development`, `~/development/.tmp`, or the repo's gitignored `.tmp/`. Spell the path out in every agent brief — there is no deny rule or hook enforcing it; that was tried and reverted.

Clean up after yourself: no orphan worktrees, branches, or temp files. Never surface cleanup as a question, just do it. Remove temp dirs with `scratch-clean <path>`, never `rm -rf` (always-ask, stalls). `scratch-clean` refuses paths outside `$HOME/development/.tmp`; don't widen it.

## Shell and language

Never use the `&` background operator — it fires an approval prompt. Use the Bash tool's `run_in_background` instead (main session only; agents run in the foreground).

No Python, ever. Node/TypeScript for servers, tooling, utilities and one-off glue. Where there is no Node equivalent, prefer a CLI tool (ffmpeg, ImageMagick). Say this in every agent brief that involves scripting.

Never open tmux sessions or split panes. Servers, watchers, tests and demos all run headless. This host is on a tailnet — bind services to `0.0.0.0` and print links as `<hostname>:<port>` or the tailnet URL.

## Git and work boundaries

Always pull latest main. Cut new worktrees from a fresh pull; never interfere with other work.

Stay in your lane. A CI red in a package this workstream doesn't touch is external — rerun if plausibly transient, otherwise wait or report. Never dispatch a fix into it, never push to a branch this session didn't create. An **assigned** ticket is someone else's, full stop.

## Building

Use package scripts and make commands; add new ones as needed. Always run the formatter — usually `npm run fix`.

Every regression he reports ships with a CI regression test that fails before the fix and passes after. State which test now covers it.

"Implement this epic end-to-end" INCLUDES the CDK and infrastructure — stacks, pipelines, cross-account wiring, config. The epic-e2e ask IS the explicit approval the CDK rule otherwise requires; don't carve infra out as a follow-up or stop to re-ask. Deliver the feature working in the deployed system, not just the application code.

Don't hack around a failure to get it working. Never bypass CI or code-quality gates.

## Writing and GitHub etiquette

Anything a human reads and judges — issues, PR descriptions, review replies, RFC/EDD/ADR text, Jira stories, docs — follows `~/.claude/agents/writer.md`: the voice, the per-format word budgets, the banned list, the four deslop passes. Read it before drafting anything longer than a sentence. Write the intent, not the mechanics; never describe how you got there or what you did not do.

Never commit a new EDD or design doc to the repo — post it as a GitHub issue and link it from PRs. Committed EDDs go stale and get read as current truth; treat existing repo EDDs as suspect.

Never comment on GitHub issues. Everything runs under his account, so it reads as him narrating to himself. Findings go in our own PR body, or to him in chat or Slack.

PR screenshots use the `screenshot` skill (orphan branch recipe).

Never publish from this machine — packages, docs, deploys, anything outward-facing. Merging the PR **is** the publish step.

## Credentials

`AWS_PROFILE` comes from the repo's `.envrc`; use it with the AWS CLI or SDK. When credentials expire, the main session uses `/sso` — agents never do (see `agent-execution.md`).
# Running builds, tests and installs as an agent

Read this before the first build, typecheck, test or install inside a worktree. It is the *how* for the runs you actually need — it is not a reason to run more of them. CI runs the full suite on every PR; local runs exist to debug a specific failure, never to gate a push.

## Wrappers a hook enforces

Every build, typecheck and test goes through `cap` (`cap npm run build`), or `vtest` for vitest (`vtest npm test`). They impose a hard memory ceiling, deny swap, and kill on a wall clock. A hook refuses the uncapped form.

`node --test` needs an explicit finite `--test-timeout`; it defaults to Infinity, and one such run held 7.7 GB for two hours and wedged the host.

Never raise `VITEST_WORKERS`. Never start vitest in watch mode — no `test:watch`, no `vitest --watch`, no `--ui`. An abandoned watcher parks its worker processes forever with nobody left to stop them, and that has taken the host down.

## Every worktree installs, where the registry is public

In reader and any other repo that installs from the public registry, a new worktree starts with its own install, the way CI does. `worktree-setup` does the whole bootstrap — fetch, worktree, install — and is on PATH:

```bash
worktree-setup ~/development/reader ~/development/reader-worktrees/<name> <branch>
```

It fetches `origin`, cuts the worktree off `origin/main`, and installs inside it with `cap npm ci --prefer-offline` under the shared install lock. Reach for the bare install only when a worktree already exists:

```bash
cap npm ci --prefer-offline
```

The npm cache is shared across every worktree on this host, so a warm cache makes this cheap. Never borrow another checkout's `node_modules` here: it drifts from the lockfile the moment a branch touches a dependency, and the failures that produces read as bugs in the code. `node_modules` is never the problem.

The install is the heavy step. It costs ~2 GB, and parallel fanouts have OOM'd the host, so installs run **one at a time** — through `cap` where it exists, and under the shared lock when a hook denies a concurrent one:

```bash
flock ~/development/.tmp/npm-install.lock npm ci --prefer-offline
```

Never wrap it in a sleep loop.

## Where the registry needs credentials

The CodeArtifact-authed repos are the exception: `npm ci` there needs a token, and an expired one blocks the install outright. Read `codeartifact-auth.md`, make one attempt, then take one of these two routes.

**Hard-link the main checkout's install.** Valid only when your branch changes no dependency — check `git diff origin/main -- package.json package-lock.json` is empty first.

```bash
cp -al <main-checkout>/node_modules <worktree>/node_modules
```

Workspace entries are relative symlinks (`../../packages/…`), so they re-point at your own worktree's packages; the rest hard-links at near-zero disk. Never `npm ci` / `npm install` into that tree afterwards.

**If dependencies genuinely differ**, don't fight it. Write the change by reading the code, push, and let CI install and validate — it has its own credentials. Iterate on `gh run view --log-failed`; a red push is the cost of this route, not a failure. With no `node_modules` there is no build, no `tsc`, no tests and no formatter, so read surrounding call sites instead of pattern-matching, and match formatting by hand. Say in your summary that nothing was verified locally.

An auth wall is never a stop and never a Slack ping; quote the real error in your final summary and carry on.

## Missing tools

Never run or brief `sudo` or `apt-get install`; both stall on an approval prompt with nobody there to clear it. To get a tool you lack, unpack it locally:

```bash
apt-get download <pkg> && dpkg-deb -x <pkg>*.deb ./.tools
```

# Stallion

An infinite-zoom drawing board. Client: TypeScript, Preact and Vite in `apps/web`, with shared code in `packages/*`. Server: a Rust Cloudflare Worker in `crates/server`, built with `worker-build` for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

## Rules

- TypeScript and Rust only. No Python.
- One PR per stage, in issue order.
- npm workspaces with one lockfile at the root. Current major versions of every tool.
- Biome formats and lints TypeScript; `cargo fmt` and `clippy` cover Rust. Run `npm run fix` before every commit.
- Minimal tests, speed over coverage: Vitest with a smoke test per package, `cargo test` for the crate. No coverage thresholds; Playwright only drives `npm run smoke`.
- CI is one fast job. It is the test runner; push instead of running suites locally.

## Scripts

| Script | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run fix` | Biome and `cargo fmt` rewrite files |
| `npm run lint` / `lint:rust` | Biome check / `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy -D warnings` |
| `npm run typecheck` | `tsc` over every package |
| `npm test` / `test:rust` | Vitest / `cargo test` |
| `npm run build` / `build:worker` | Vite build of `apps/web` / wasm bundle in `crates/server/build`; `build:worker` installs rustup, the toolchain and `worker-build` when missing |
| `npm run deploy` | `wrangler deploy` with the Access vars from the committed state; refuses to run outside Workers Builds |
| `npm run wait:live -- <sha> [origin]` | Poll `/api/me/boards` through Access until `x-stallion-commit` equals the sha, at most 15 minutes |
| `npm run smoke -- [--pull] [url]` | One real page load on a touch tablet, light and dark: draw, reload, check the stroke |
| `npm run demo:duo -- <url> [--board <id>]` | Two 1280x800 browsers on one board: A draws blue, B draws red on top; checks each sees the other's ink and both read Connected. Videos, a side-by-side `combined.mp4` and screenshots land in `~/development/.tmp/stallion-duo/<timestamp>/` |
| `npm run access:env` | Write the Access service token from `tofu output` into `~/.config/stallion/access-env` (mode 600); prints nothing |
| `npm run icons -w @stallion/web` | Regenerate the PWA icons in `apps/web/public/icons` with sharp |
| `npm run serve:sync` | Build `apps/web` against the local worker and serve both with `wrangler dev` on port 8787 |

`wrangler.jsonc` runs the worker from `crates/server/build` and serves `apps/web/dist` as static assets.

## Sync URL

The Worker serves both the assets and the WebSocket, so the client needs no build-time config in production. `syncUrlFor()` in `apps/web/src/sync.ts` picks the sync server once per board:

1. `VITE_SYNC_URL`, when it was set at build time (`npm run serve:sync` sets it to the local worker).
2. Otherwise local only, when the page is on localhost, a private LAN address, a tailnet address (`100.64.0.0/10`) or `*.ts.net`. That is the Vite dev server.
3. Otherwise the page's own origin, `wss://<host>` (or `ws://` over http). `openBoard` appends `/api/boards/<boardId>/ws`.

Workers Builds builds without `VITE_SYNC_URL`, so the deployed app syncs with the Worker that served it.

## Smoke

After pushing to main, run `npm run smoke -- --pull` and paste its result in the final summary. It fast-forwards `~/development/stallion`, reinstalls, then loads the live dev server (default `http://100.104.44.51:5173/b/<fresh id>`, a new board each run) headless on a Galaxy Tab S9 viewport in light and dark, draws one touch stroke, reloads and checks the stroke is stored and visible. Any console error or failed request fails it. Screenshots land in `~/development/.tmp/stallion-smoke/<timestamp>/`. A push is not done until the smoke passes.

Against the deployed Worker, run `npm run access:env` once, then `npm run smoke -- https://stallion.matthijs-f49.workers.dev/b/<id>` or `npm run demo:duo -- https://stallion.matthijs-f49.workers.dev/`. Both scripts read `CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_ID` and `CF_ACCESS_CLIENT_SECRET` from the environment, else from `~/.config/stallion/access-env`, and send them as `CF-Access-Client-Id` and `CF-Access-Client-Secret` on every request of every browser context. The `smoke` job in `deploy.yml` runs the same smoke on `/b/ci-<run id>` once the live Worker serves the pushed commit, reading both values from the committed state outputs; a failing smoke fails the workflow.

## Deploy

Cloudflare Workers Builds deploys the `stallion` Worker on every push to `main`; GitHub holds no deploy credentials. The build is connected to this repository in the Worker's Settings, Builds, with root directory `/`, build command `npm run build && npm run build:worker` and deploy command `npm run deploy`. Non-production branch builds are off. The build image has Node but no Rust, so `npm-scripts/build-worker.sh` installs rustup, the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml` and `worker-build` on every build; the build cache keeps only npm. `npm run deploy` passes `ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN` and `ACCESS_AUD` from the committed `infra/terraform.tfstate` to `wrangler deploy --var`, so an Access change reaches the Worker on the push that commits the new state.

`crates/server/build.rs` bakes `WORKERS_CI_COMMIT_SHA`, else `git rev-parse HEAD`, into the Worker, which answers every request it handles with `x-stallion-commit`. Assets are served before the Worker, so only `/api/*` carries the header. The `smoke` job in `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` runs on every push to `main`: it waits up to 15 minutes for that header to equal the pushed sha, then runs the smoke through Access. A newer push cancels the older smoke. `npm run deploy:dry` validates the bundle locally without deploying.

The Worker needs one secret, `BOARD_PASS_SECRET`, the HMAC key for board passes. Set it once per Worker with `wrangler secret put BOARD_PASS_SECRET`, piping 32 random bytes as hex; it survives deploys. For `wrangler dev`, put it in a gitignored `.dev.vars`. Without it, open boards still sync, but setting a PIN or joining a locked board answers 500 `PassSecretMissing`.

## PWA

`vite-plugin-pwa` builds the manifest and a Workbox service worker from `apps/web/pwa.config.ts`. The worker precaches the built shell and assets and serves `index.html` for navigations to `/` and `/b/*`, the slugged form included; it has no runtime routes, so `/api/*` and the sync WebSocket always go to the network. `apps/web/public/_headers` sets `Cache-Control: no-cache` on `sw.js` and the manifest.

## Access

Cloudflare Access guards the app. The Worker verifies the RS256 JWT from the `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` header or the `CF_Authorization` cookie on every `/api/*` request: signature against the team keys at `https://<ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN>/cdn-cgi/access/certs` (cached for an hour per isolate), `aud` against `ACCESS_AUD`, `iss` and `exp`. Anything else gets a 401. A service token JWT has no email; the Worker uses its `common_name` (the client id) instead, and rejects a token with neither. The verified name reaches the `Board` in the `X-Stallion-User` header, and the server writes it into every awareness state from that socket as `user.name`.

Both vars stay empty in `wrangler.jsonc`, so `wrangler dev` skips the check and logs once that Access is disabled. `npm run deploy` passes the OpenTofu outputs to `wrangler deploy --var`: `ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN` is `<team>.cloudflareaccess.com` and `ACCESS_AUD` is the application audience tag. Setting only one is an error.

## Infra

OpenTofu in `infra/` manages Cloudflare Access with the `cloudflare/cloudflare` v5 provider: the Zero Trust organization (imported; its name and team domain stay as they are), a one-time PIN identity provider, a self-hosted Access application for the Worker hostname with a 720h session that redirects straight to that provider, an `anyone-with-email` allow policy that includes `everyone`, and a second `non_identity` policy for the `stallion-automation` service token that the smoke and duo demo use. The token lasts 8760h; bump `client_secret_version` to rotate it. Nothing is changed in the dashboard.

Anyone who can receive a one-time PIN at any email address can log in; no email address lives in the repo or the state. Board PINs are the real gate.

Apply is local. `npm run infra:plan` and `npm run infra:apply` run `tofu init` and the command in `infra/`, reading `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` from `~/.config/stallion/cf-env`. After an apply, commit `infra/terraform.tfstate` and push it to `main`; that push redeploys the Worker with the new outputs. The state is the only record of what exists; never delete or hand-edit it. The state holds the service token client secret in plain text and is committed to this private repo, so anyone who can read the repo can pass Access as the automation token. That is accepted for now.

The `infra` job in `deploy.yml` runs `tofu plan` on pull requests that touch `infra/` and nothing else; CI never applies.

The `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` Actions secret serves that plan, and the local token in `cf-env` serves the apply. Both need these permissions, as the API token editor names them:

- Account, Access: Organizations, Identity Providers, and Groups, Edit
- Account, Access: Apps and Policies, Edit
- Account, Access: Service Tokens, Edit
- Account, Workers Scripts, Edit
- User, User Details, Read

## Board URLs

A board id is 128 random bits from `crypto.getRandomValues`, base36 lower case, zero-padded to 25 characters (`randomBoardId()` in `apps/web/src/id.ts`). The client and server accept `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`, so older ids such as `default` still open. The app routes `/b/:id` and `/b/:id/:slug` on the id alone; the slug is the board name lower-cased, runs of anything but ascii letters and digits turned into `-`, trimmed, at most 60 characters, and left off while the name is empty or still the id. On open and after a rename in the Share panel, `history.replaceState` rewrites the address to `/b/<id>/<slug>`. The Share link, its QR code and the landing rows carry the slug; the REST and WebSocket paths carry the id only.

## Wire protocol

One Durable Object (`Board`) per board, reached at `GET /api/boards/{boardId}/ws` with a WebSocket upgrade. The same object serves the PIN routes below. Sockets use the hibernation API; each socket's subscriptions and awareness client ids live in its attachment. Tile docs load lazily from SQLite (`Storage::sql()` in `worker` 0.8.6, `new_sqlite_classes`) on first use. The `tile` table holds each doc as one compacted yrs update and `object_index` holds each object's bbox as JSON `[minX,minY,maxX,maxY]`; the `schema_migration` table records applied migrations. An alarm flushes dirty tiles 5 s after the first change, then evicts tiles idle for 60 s.

Every message is one binary CBOR map `{tileKey, kind, payload}`. `payload` is a plain byte string (cbor-x `tagUint8Array: false`; the server also accepts tag 64). `encodeFrame` and `decodeFrame` in `packages/schema` are the client codec; `fixtures/frame.cbor.hex` pins the bytes for both sides.

| kind | tileKey | payload | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Subscribe` | `level:tx:ty` | empty | client to server; the server replies with `Sync` step 1 |
| `Unsubscribe` | `level:tx:ty` | empty | client to server |
| `Sync` | `level:tx:ty` | one y-protocols sync message (`writeSyncStep1`, `writeSyncStep2` or `writeUpdate`) | both ways |
| `Awareness` | `""` | `encodeAwarenessUpdate` output | both ways, board-wide |
| `View` | `""` | CBOR map `{minX, minY, maxX, maxY, zoom}`: world bounds of the viewport | client to server |
| `Snapshot` | `level:tx:ty` | the tile doc as one yrs update, read-only | server to client |
| `Move` | `""` | CBOR map `{objectId, fromTile, toTile, fromUpdate, toUpdate}`: one Yjs update per tile | client to server |
| `Reject` | the frame's tileKey | UTF-8 reason | server to client |

- A `View` replaces the socket's view. `viewTiles()` from `packages/geometry` splits it into levels; `crates/server/src/view.rs` mirrors that maths, and a cargo test checks both sides use the same constants. The live band (tiles of 64 px and up) is subscribed by range, so a tile that leaves the view is unsubscribed, explicit `Subscribe`s outside the band included. The server flushes dirty tiles, then runs one `object_index` range query per level, coarse first and nearest the centre first, until the view holds 4096 objects. A newly live tile with objects gets `Sync` step 1 and step 2; a finer tile gets a `Snapshot`, resent on every `View`. A live tile cut by the budget stays subscribed and syncs on the client's step 1. Bounds must be finite and at most 16384 px a side on screen.
- A tile key is `tileKey()` from `packages/geometry`, level -40..40. `Sync` on an unsubscribed tile is rejected.
- A tile doc holds one root, the `Y.Map` `objects`, keyed by `objectId`. Each value is the `encode()` CBOR of the object as a `Uint8Array`. The server validates every changed value with serde and rejects the whole update if one fails.
- The server relays accepted step 2 and update messages as `writeUpdate` to the tile's other subscribers. An update with missing dependencies is not applied; the server answers with its own step 1 and the client replies with step 2.
- A `Move` carries an object across a tile or level: `fromUpdate` deletes it from `fromTile`, `toUpdate` sets it in `toTile`. Both tiles must be subscribed. The server validates both updates and applies both or neither, relays each as a `Sync` update, and flushes the dirty set in one synchronous write, which the Durable Object commits as one transaction. `put` in `packages/client-sync` sends a `Move` when an object changes tile; offline, it queues the delete before the insert. `fixtures/move.cbor.hex` pins the payload.
- An object lives in exactly one tile. A move beats a concurrent edit that kept the object in the source tile, and the first of two concurrent moves wins: when an update brings an object into a tile while another tile, loaded or in `object_index`, still holds it, the server deletes the newcomer and sends that delete to every subscriber, the sender included.
- On connect the server sends the board's awareness states; on close it broadcasts their removal.
- A text frame or undecodable CBOR closes the socket with 1003 or 1007.

### Board PIN

A board is open to anyone with its link until a PIN is set. The PIN is 6 digits, stored in the `board_lock` table as `pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash>` (WebCrypto PBKDF2-SHA256, 100000 iterations, 16-byte salt, base64url) with a `generation` that grows on every change. Every refusal is JSON `{reason, message}`.

| Route | Body | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/boards/{boardId}/ws?pass=<pass>` | | On a locked board, 403 `PinRequired` without a pass or 403 `PassInvalid` with a bad one, before the upgrade check. A plain GET that passes the lock gets 426; the client uses that as its probe after a refused handshake. |
| `POST /api/boards/{boardId}/join` | `{"pin": "123456"}` | 200 `{pinSet, pass, expiresAt}`; 403 `WrongPin`, 400 `InvalidPin`, 429 `RateLimited` with `Retry-After`. Five attempts a minute per client, keyed by the Access email, else `CF-Connecting-IP`, kept in `pin_attempt`. |
| `POST /api/boards/{boardId}/pin` | `{"pin": "123456"}`, or `""` to remove | Allowed on an open board, or with a valid pass in `X-Stallion-Pass`. Setting answers `{pinSet: true, pass, expiresAt}` and closes every socket with 4003, so each reconnects through the lock; removing answers `{pinSet: false}`. |
| `GET /api/boards/{boardId}/pin` | | `{pinSet}` |

A pass is `base64url(JSON {boardId, exp, generation}).base64url(HMAC-SHA256(BOARD_PASS_SECRET, first part))`. `exp` is Unix seconds, 30 days after issue. A pass is valid for its board until it expires or the PIN changes. The client keeps it in `localStorage` under `stallion:pass:<boardId>`, sends it as `?pass=` on the socket, and drops it on `PassInvalid`. After a refused handshake `openBoard` probes the socket URL over HTTP; a 403 lock reason sets status `NeedsPin` and stops retrying until `join()` stores a pass and reconnects.

### My boards

One `UserIndex` Durable Object per verified identity (the Access email, the service token common name, or `local` when Access is disabled) keeps that user's board list in its `my_board` table, capped at the 200 most recently opened. A removal is a tombstone: the row stays with `removed_at` set (Unix ms, 0 while listed) and its thumbnail cleared, so a device that still holds the board cannot merge it back. Tombstones older than 90 days are purged on the next request; they do not count against the cap.

| Route | Body | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/me/boards` | | `[{boardId, name, lastOpened, thumbnail, removedAt}]`, newest `lastOpened` first; tombstones included with `removedAt` > 0 |
| `PUT /api/me/boards/{boardId}` | `{name?, lastOpened?, thumbnail?}` | The upserted row. `lastOpened` (Unix ms) never moves back; a new row defaults to now and its id as name. On a tombstone, only a `lastOpened` newer than `removedAt` revives the row; anything else updates it and leaves it removed. A thumbnail is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL of at most 24 KB: 413 `ThumbnailTooLarge`, 400 `ThumbnailNotPng`. |
| `DELETE /api/me/boards/{boardId}` | | 204; records a tombstone at the server's now, also for a board the list never held |
| `GET /api/me/ws` | | WebSocket upgrade (426 without one), hibernation API. The server pushes one binary CBOR map `{kind: "boards", rows, thumbnails}` on connect and after every accepted `PUT` or `DELETE`, to every open socket of that identity; `rows` is what `GET /api/me/boards` answers. When the frame would exceed 256 KB the rows go with empty thumbnails and `thumbnails: false`, and the client fetches the list over REST. The client sends nothing; a text frame closes it with 1003. |

`myBoards()` in `packages/client-sync` wraps the three routes; `subscribe(listener)` opens the socket with the board socket's reconnect and backoff and hands each pushed list to the listener, and `close()` tears it down. The landing page merges the server list with the device list on load (newest `lastOpened` per board; the server's name unless this device renamed it since the last sync) and writes the result back to both. A tombstone drops the device's entry unless this device opened the board after `removedAt`, in which case the merge pushes that `lastOpened` and the server revives the row. After that first sync the landing page subscribes, merges every pushed list into the device list by the same rule and re-renders in place; the dot in its header shows the socket state with the board page's colours. Opening a board upserts `lastOpened`; its thumbnail uploads at most once per 10 s and when the board closes.

- One PR per stage, in issue order.
- npm workspaces with one lockfile at the root. Current major versions of every tool.
- Biome formats and lints TypeScript; `cargo fmt` and `clippy` cover Rust. Run `npm run fix` before every commit.
- Minimal tests, speed over coverage: Vitest with a smoke test per package, `cargo test` for the crate. No coverage thresholds; Playwright only drives `npm run smoke`.
- CI is one fast job. It is the test runner; push instead of running suites locally.

## Scripts

| Script | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run fix` | Biome and `cargo fmt` rewrite files |
| `npm run lint` / `lint:rust` | Biome check / `cargo fmt --check` and `clippy -D warnings` |
| `npm run typecheck` | `tsc` over every package |
| `npm test` / `test:rust` | Vitest / `cargo test` |
| `npm run build` / `build:worker` | Vite build of `apps/web` / wasm bundle in `crates/server/build`; `build:worker` installs rustup, the toolchain and `worker-build` when missing |
| `npm run deploy` | `wrangler deploy` with the Access vars from the committed state; refuses to run outside Workers Builds |
| `npm run wait:live -- <sha> [origin]` | Poll `/api/me/boards` through Access until `x-stallion-commit` equals the sha, at most 15 minutes |
| `npm run smoke -- [--pull] [url]` | One real page load on a touch tablet, light and dark: draw, reload, check the stroke |
| `npm run demo:duo -- <url> [--board <id>]` | Two 1280x800 browsers on one board: A draws blue, B draws red on top; checks each sees the other's ink and both read Connected. Videos, a side-by-side `combined.mp4` and screenshots land in `~/development/.tmp/stallion-duo/<timestamp>/` |
| `npm run access:env` | Write the Access service token from `tofu output` into `~/.config/stallion/access-env` (mode 600); prints nothing |

After pushing to main, run `npm run smoke -- --pull` and paste its result in the final summary. ## Deploy

Cloudflare Workers Builds deploys the `stallion` Worker on every push to `main`; GitHub holds no deploy credentials. The build is connected to this repository in the Worker's Settings, Builds, with root directory `/`, build command `npm run build && npm run build:worker` and deploy command `npm run deploy`. Non-production branch builds are off. `crates/server/build.rs` bakes `WORKERS_CI_COMMIT_SHA`, else `git rev-parse HEAD`, into the Worker, which answers every request it handles with `x-stallion-commit`. The Worker needs one secret, `BOARD_PASS_SECRET`, the HMAC key for board passes. `vite-plugin-pwa` builds the manifest and a Workbox service worker from `apps/web/pwa.config.ts`. The worker precaches the built shell and assets and serves `index.html` for navigations to `/` and `/b/*`, the slugged form included; it has no runtime routes, so `/api/*` and the sync WebSocket always go to the network. `apps/web/public/_headers` sets `Cache-Control: no-cache` on `sw.js` and the manifest.

Cloudflare Access guards the app. The Worker verifies the RS256 JWT from the `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` header or the `CF_Authorization` cookie on every `/api/*` request: signature against the team keys at `https://<ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN>/cdn-cgi/access/certs` (cached for an hour per isolate), `aud` against `ACCESS_AUD`, `iss` and `exp`. OpenTofu in `infra/` manages Cloudflare Access with the `cloudflare/cloudflare` v5 provider: the Zero Trust organization (imported; its name and team domain stay as they are), a one-time PIN identity provider, a self-hosted Access application for the Worker hostname with a 720h session that redirects straight to that provider, an `anyone-with-email` allow policy that includes `everyone`, and a second `non_identity` policy for the `stallion-automation` service token that the smoke and duo demo use. Anyone who can receive a one-time PIN at any email address can log in; no email address lives in the repo or the state. Board PINs are the real gate.

Apply is local. `npm run infra:plan` and `npm run infra:apply` run `tofu init` and the command in `infra/`, reading `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` from `~/.config/stallion/cf-env`. The state holds the service token client secret in plain text and is committed to this private repo, so anyone who can read the repo can pass Access as the automation token. That is accepted for now.

The `infra` job in `deploy.yml` runs `tofu plan` on pull requests that touch `infra/` and nothing else; CI never applies.

The `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` Actions secret serves that plan, and the local token in `cf-env` serves the apply. Both need these permissions, as the API token editor names them:

- Account, Access: Organizations, Identity Providers, and Groups, Edit
- Account, Access: Apps and Policies, Edit
- Account, Access: Service Tokens, Edit
- Account, Workers Scripts, Edit
- User, User Details, Read

The client keeps it in `localStorage` under `stallion:pass:<boardId>`, sends it as `?pass=` on the socket, and drops it on `PassInvalid`. After a refused handshake `openBoard` probes the socket URL over HTTP; a 403 lock reason sets status `NeedsPin` and stops retrying until `join()` stores a pass and reconnects.

One `UserIndex` Durable Object per verified identity (the Access email, the service token common name, or `local` when Access is disabled) keeps that user's board list in its `my_board` table, capped at the 200 most recently opened. A removal is a tombstone: the row stays with `removed_at` set (Unix ms, 0 while listed) and its thumbnail cleared, so a device that still holds the board cannot merge it back. Tombstones older than 90 days are purged on the next request; they do not count against the cap.

| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/me/boards` | | `[{boardId, name, lastOpened, thumbnail, removedAt}]`, newest `lastOpened` first; tombstones included with `removedAt` > 0 |
| `PUT /api/me/boards/{boardId}` | `{name?, lastOpened?, thumbnail?}` | The upserted row. `lastOpened` (Unix ms) never moves back; a new row defaults to now and its id as name. On a tombstone, only a `lastOpened` newer than `removedAt` revives the row; anything else updates it and leaves it removed. A thumbnail is a `data:image/png;base64,` URL of at most 24 KB: 413 `ThumbnailTooLarge`, 400 `ThumbnailNotPng`. |
| `DELETE /api/me/boards/{boardId}` | | 204; records a tombstone at the server's now, also for a board the list never held |
| `GET /api/me/ws` | | WebSocket upgrade (426 without one), hibernation API. The server pushes one binary CBOR map `{kind: "boards", rows, thumbnails}` on connect and after every accepted `PUT` or `DELETE`, to every open socket of that identity; `rows` is what `GET /api/me/boards` answers. When the frame would exceed 256 KB the rows go with empty thumbnails and `thumbnails: false`, and the client fetches the list over REST. The client sends nothing; a text frame closes it with 1003. |

`myBoards()` in `packages/client-sync` wraps the three routes; `subscribe(listener)` opens the socket with the board socket's reconnect and backoff and hands each pushed list to the listener, and `close()` tears it down. The landing page merges the server list with the device list on load (newest `lastOpened` per board; the server's name unless this device renamed it since the last sync) and writes the result back to both. A tombstone drops the device's entry unless this device opened the board after `removedAt`, in which case the merge pushes that `lastOpened` and the server revives the row. After that first sync the landing page subscribes, merges every pushed list into the device list by the same rule and re-renders in place; the dot in its header shows the socket state with the board page's colours. Opening a board upserts `lastOpened`; its thumbnail uploads at most once per 10 s and when the board closes.

You are a silent background devops engineer executing one delegated task end-to-end, scoped to `deploy/**`, docker-compose files, installer/updater shell, and `npm-scripts/**`.

Operating rules (non-negotiable):

- Stop EXACTLY ONCE, with a short final summary: PR/commit URL + one line. No interim status, no questions mid-task, no essays. Never reply with a bare "." — that convention belongs to the main session.
- Do the work YOURSELF. Never spawn sub-agents or delegate — an agent that delegates creates relay chains that burn tokens and lose accountability.
- NEVER stop to wait. No `run_in_background` Bash, no monitors, no "resume when notified". Run long commands (tests, builds) in the foreground with a 600000ms timeout; rerun in chunks if a run needs longer.
- Read the repo's AGENTS.md (if present) before starting and follow it.
- Work in a fresh worktree on a NEW branch cut from latest origin/main — always `git fetch origin` first, then `git worktree add ~/development/<repo>-worktrees/<name> -b <branch> origin/main`. Never branch from a stale local main, never reuse an existing branch or worktree, never touch the main checkout. Remove your worktree when done; keep the pushed branch.
- Scratch files go in the repo's .tmp/ (gitignored) or ~/development/.tmp — never /tmp.
- Never open tmux sessions or split panes; run everything headless.
- **Push first; CI is the only test runner.** As soon as the change compiles and the formatter has run: commit, push, open the PR. NEVER run test suites locally — no package suites, no stack tests, no "verify locally" pass; duplicating CI wastes tokens and wall-clock. The one exception: debugging a SPECIFIC test CI already reported failing — run only that test, fix, push.
- **Stop when the PR is open.** Never wait for CI, a Copilot review, or any check; the main session watches the PR and resumes you with anything to fix. Only when resumed with a specific failure or thread do you fix it, push, and stop again.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work.
